newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea formally launches fresh probe into Hanbo.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea formally launches fresh probe into Hanbo.

text.p: South Korea's parliament on Monday formally launched a fresh probe into the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co following opposition accusations that prosecutors are not revealing all they know about the scandal.
Parliamentary speaker Kim Soo-han accepted a joint request by South Korea's three main parties that the National Assembly form a special committee for a 45-day probe.

"We will shed light on the real truth of 'Hanbogate'," said Cho Se-hyong, a member of parliament from the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, referring to the scandal swirling around Hanbo Steel.
The steelmaking flagship of the Hanbo Group, South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate, was declared insolvent on January 23 after racking up five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans.

Opposition parties have accused prosecutors of trying to wind down their investigation into the loans without identifying the "real big shots" who pressured banks into offering loans that make no economic sense.
Cho said his National Congress planned to call Kim Hyun-chul, President Kim Young-sam's son, to a parliamentary hearing over the loans. Kim Hyun-chul has said he has nothing to do with Hanbo's loans.
Prosecutors said on Sunday they would soon question Kim Hyun-chul. But they told reporters on Monday they would release details on their probe on Wednesday without questioning him.
Senior prosecutor Choi Byung-koog said the reversal was due to a decision by Kim Hyun-chul to delay filing a criminal libel complaint.
"Kim Hyun-chul has not yet filed a complaint," a prosecution official told Reuters by telephone. "Questioning him would only take place after he lodges the complaint."

The president's son had earlier said he would file the complaint on Monday against two National Congress lawmakers who accused him of peddling influence in giving loans to Hanbo. The two alleged they had evidence he maintained links to Hanbo.
"National Congress has so far failed to produce evidence (implicating Kim Hyun-chul) but made up and spread groundless rumours," the ruling party spokesman said.
Speculation Kim Hyun-chul maintained close links with Hanbo was fanned by Saturday's discovery of more than 10,000 copies of a book written by him in a Hanbo Group warehouse in Seoul.
The opposition has said the books found in the warehouse highlighted that Hanbo had been a sponsor of Kim Hyun-chul.
A National Congress statement said on Monday: "Prosecutors are dancing to Kim Hyun-chul's tunes. They are not fit to investigate him. They'll find out nothing and will try to give him an acquittal."
Ruling New Korea Party spokesman Kim Chul said his party agreed to the parliamentary probe into the scandal, which the president has called a typical example of corruption.
The United Liberal Democratic Party, which together with the New Korea Party control all but 11 of the 299 parliamentary seats, also agreed to the new investigation.
On Friday, state prosecutors said a three-week investigation into the Hanbo case was approaching an end with a clutch of President Kim's closest political allies and top bankers in custody.

Those held are a former cabinet minister and three lawmakers from the ruling party -- two of them Kim's top loyalists -- one opposition member of parliament, two bankers, the founder of Hanbo Group and his former executive.
